In North America, the thesis defense or oral defense is the final examination for <color=#3366CC>doctoral</color> candidates, and sometimes for
<color=#3366CC>master's</color> candidates.
The examining committee normally consists of the thesis committee, usually a given number of professors mainly from
the student's university plus their primary supervisor, an external examiner (someone not otherwise connected to the
university), and a chair person. Each committee member will have been given a completed copy of the dissertation
prior to the defense, and will come prepared to ask questions about the thesis itself and the subject matter. In many
schools, master's thesis defenses are restricted to the examinee and the examiners, but doctoral defenses are open to
the public.
The typical format will see the candidate giving a short (20–40-minute) presentation of their research, followed by one
to two hours of questions.
At some U.S. institutions, a longer public lecture (known as a "thesis talk" or "thesis seminar") by the candidate will
accompany the defense itself, in which case only the candidate, the examiners, and other members of the faculty may
attend the actual defense.
Norway
In Norway, the final examination for a PhD student is called a disputas. The examination consists of a public lecture by
the candidate where the audience can ask questions. Then two opponents will ask the candidate questions. Prior to the
examination, the candidate must pass a trial lecture on a topic typically not part of the student's research. This is used
to assess the candidate's ability to find the relevant literature and to disseminate knowledge to an audience.
Russia and Ukraine
A student in Russia or Ukraine has to complete a thesis and then defend it in front of their department. Sometimes the
defense meeting is made up of the learning institute's professionals and sometimes the students peers are allowed to
view or join in. After the presentation and defense of the thesis, the final conclusion of the department should be that
none of them have reservations on the content and quality of the thesis.
A conclusion on the thesis has to be approved by the rector of the educational institute. This conclusion (final grade so
to speak) of the thesis can be defended/argued not only at the thesis council, but also in any other thesis council of
Russia or Ukraine.
Spain
The former (DEA) lasted two years and candidates were required to complete coursework and demonstrate their ability
to research the specific topics they have studied. From 2011 on, these courses were replaced by academic Master's
programmes that include specific training on epistemology, and scientific methodology. After its completion, students
are able to enroll in a specific PhD programme (programa de doctorado) and begin a dissertation on a set topic for a
maximum time of three years (full-time) and five years (part-time). All students must have a full professor as an
academic advisor (director de tesis) and a tutor, who is usually the same person.
A dissertation (tesis doctoral), with an average of 250 pages, is the main requisite along with typically one previously
published journal article. Once candidates have published their written dissertations, they will be evaluated by two
external academics (evaluadores externos) and subsequently it is usually exhibited publicly for fifteen natural days.
After its approval, candidates must defend publicly their research before a three-member committee (tribunal) with at
least one visiting academic: chair, secretary and member (presidente, secretario y vocal).
A typical public Thesis Defence (defensa) lasts 45 minutes and all attendants holding a doctoral degree are eligible to
ask questions.
United Kingdom, Ireland and Hong Kong
In Hong Kong, Ireland and the United Kingdom, the thesis defense is called a viva voce (<color=#3366CC>Latin</color> for 'by live voice')
examination (viva for short). A typical viva lasts for approximately 3 hours, though there is no formal time limit. Involved
in the viva are two examiners and the candidate. Usually, one examiner is an academic from the candidate's own
university department (but not one of the candidate's supervisors) and the other is an external examiner from a different
university. Increasingly, the examination may involve a third academic, the 'chair'; this person, from the candidate's
institution, acts as an impartial observer with oversight of the examination process to ensure that the examination is
fair. The 'chair' does not ask academic questions of the candidate.
In the United Kingdom, there are only two or at most three examiners, and in many universities the examination is held
in private. The candidate's primary supervisor is not permitted to ask or answer questions during the viva, and their
presence is not necessary. However, some universities permit members of the faculty or the university to attend. At the
University of Oxford, for instance, any member of the university may attend a DPhil viva (the university's regulations
require that details of the examination and its time and place be published formally in advance) provided they attend in
full academic dress.
Submission
A submission of the thesis is the last formal requirement for most students after the defense. By the final deadline, the
student must submit a complete copy of the thesis to the appropriate body within the accepting institution, along with
the appropriate forms, bearing the signatures of the primary supervisor, the examiners, and in some cases, the head of
the student's department. Other required forms may include library authorizations (giving the university library
permission to make the thesis available as part of its collection) and <color=#3366CC>copyright</color> permissions (in the event that the student
has incorporated copyrighted materials in the thesis). Many large scientific publishing houses (e.g. Taylor & Francis,
Elsevier) use copyright agreements that allow the authors to incorporate their published articles into dissertations
without separate authorization. Once all the paperwork is in order, copies of the thesis may be made available in one or
more university <color=#3366CC>libraries</color>. Specialist abstracting services exist to publicize the content of these beyond the institutions in
which they are produced. Many institutions now insist on submission of digitized as well as, or even in lieu of, printed
copies of theses; the digitized versions of successful theses are often made available online.
History of Europe
The history of Europe can be traced back to the appearance of the <color=#3366CC>first modern humans</color> identified as ancestors of
contemporary Europeans about 37,000 years ago during the Paleolithic. Early European Farmers migrating from
<color=#3366CC>Anatolia</color> spread agriculture across the continent during the <color=#3366CC>Neolithic</color> (7000–2000 BC), a period that also included early
metallurgy. Starting around 4000 BC, westward migrations of steppe pastoralists spread <color=#3366CC>Indo-European</color> languages.
The rise of the city-states of <color=#3366CC>ancient Greece</color> defines the beginning of <color=#3366CC>classical antiquity</color> (c. 800 BC-AD 500). The
<color=#3366CC>Hellenistic period</color> (323–30 BC) began with <color=#3366CC>Alexander the Great</color>'s 4th-century BC conquests from Greece to India and
ended with the Roman Empire's control of the entire Mediterranean basin. Christianity emerged under Roman rule in
the 1st century AD. The <color=#3366CC>Migration Period</color> of the <color=#3366CC>Germanic peoples</color> began in the late 4th century AD.
The <color=#3366CC>fall of the Western Roman Empire</color> in 476 traditionally marks the beginning of the <color=#3366CC>Middle Ages</color> (c. 500–1500). While
the <color=#3366CC>Eastern Roman ("Byzantine") Empire</color> with its capital in <color=#3366CC>Constantinople</color> continued for another 1000 years, the former
lands of the Western Empire fragmented into the barbarian kingdoms. The 8th-century <color=#3366CC>Umayyad conquest of Hispania</color>

established <color=#3366CC>Al-Andalus</color>. The Rome-based Latin Church proclaimed the King of the <color=#3366CC>Franks</color>, <color=#3366CC>Charlemagne</color>, as <color=#3366CC>"Emperor</color>
<color=#3366CC>of the Romans"</color> in the early 9th century and increasingly competitive <color=#3366CC>missionary efforts</color> by the Latin West and
Byzantines resulted in the division of the <color=#3366CC>Slavic peoples</color> between <color=#3366CC>Latin</color> and <color=#3366CC>Cyrillic</color> use. Norsemen raided, invaded, and
trafficked slaves across Europe during the <color=#3366CC>Viking Age</color>. During the <color=#3366CC>High Middle Ages</color> (c. 1000–1300), the Latin Church
<color=#3366CC>split with the Eastern Orthodox Church</color>, was convulsed by reform and <color=#3366CC>entangled in conflict with the Holy Roman</color>
<color=#3366CC>Empire</color>, called for the <color=#3366CC>Crusades</color>, and provided key support for <color=#3366CC>northern Italian city-states</color> achieving independence from
the Empire. The oldest university currently in continuous operation in the world was established in the 12th century
amid rapid population and urban growth that continued until the end of the 13th century. Despite a decline in population
caused by the Great Famine and the <color=#3366CC>Black Death</color> in the 14th century, Europe experienced a cultural <color=#3366CC>Renaissance</color> in
the 15th century.
Early modern Europe began with 15th-century revolutions in both <color=#3366CC>printing</color> and <color=#3366CC>seafaring</color>. Printing changed how
<color=#3366CC>knowledge was created, preserved and disseminated</color> while the <color=#3366CC>Age of Discovery</color> led to extensive colonization, the
<color=#3366CC>Atlantic slave trade</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Columbian exchange</color>. The 16th-century <color=#3366CC>Reformation</color> challenged the hegemony of the

<color=#3366CC>Catholic Church</color> and precipitated <color=#3366CC>over a century of religious wars</color>. With leadership from Italian <color=#3366CC>astronomer</color> <color=#3366CC>Galileo</color>

<color=#3366CC>Galilei</color> and English <color=#3366CC>mathematical physicist</color> <color=#3366CC>Isaac Newton</color>, modern science emerged during the <color=#3366CC>Scientific Revolution</color> of
the 17th century.
The <color=#3366CC>Industrial Revolution</color> and <color=#3366CC>waves of liberal and nationalist upheaval</color> shaped the long 19th century dominated by the
five great powers of the <color=#3366CC>Concert of Europe</color>. Two rival military alliances fought <color=#3366CC>World War I</color> (1914–1918), which ended

with multi-ethnic empires fragmented into <color=#3366CC>nation states</color>. <color=#3366CC>Nazi Germany</color>'s <color=#3366CC>invasion of Poland</color> launched <color=#3366CC>World War II</color>
(1939–1945), and as its armies overran Europe the regime systematically perpetrated <color=#3366CC>the Holocaust</color>. During the <color=#3366CC>Cold</color>
<color=#3366CC>War</color> (1947–1991), Europe was divided between a <color=#3366CC>U.S.</color>-led Western bloc of countries and the <color=#3366CC>NATO</color> military alliance

and the <color=#3366CC>Soviet</color>-led <color=#3366CC>Eastern bloc</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Warsaw Pact</color>. The Western bloc's <color=#3366CC>colonial empires</color> and remaining military
dictatorships in Portugal, <color=#3366CC>Greece</color> and <color=#3366CC>Spain</color> were dismantled. After Soviet leader <color=#3366CC>Mikhail Gorbachev</color> refused to
intervene militarily against democratic reforms in Poland and elsewhere, the <color=#3366CC>Revolutions of 1989</color> led to all European
communist states transitioning to <color=#3366CC>market economies</color> and then the <color=#3366CC>Soviet Union itself dissolving</color>. The <color=#3366CC>European Union</color>
("EU") was established in 1993. In the 21st century, most of the former communist states joined the EU and Europe
faced the <color=#3366CC>Euro area crisis</color> (2009–2018) and the Russian invasion of Ukraine (2022–).
Prehistoric Europe
<color=#3366CC>Prehistoric Europe</color> refers to the earliest era of human life in Europe predating any written records.
Paleolithic and Mesolithic
The Paleolithic ("Old Stone Age") and <color=#3366CC>Mesolithic</color> ("Middle of Stone Age") eras in Europe were defined by a
<color=#3366CC>hunter-gatherer</color> way of life and an increasingly sophisticated stone-tool repertoire. Kostenki 14, an individual who lived
in the <color=#3366CC>Don River</color> basin around 37,000 years ago, is among the earliest Europeans whose genome carries an ancestry
signature recognizable in contemporary populations of the continent. The <color=#3366CC>Last Glacial Maximum</color>, roughly 27,000 to
19,000 years ago, pushed populations into southern refugia and may have reduced the human population of Europe to
as few as 20,000 people. The Western Hunter-Gatherers, who would later dominate the continent and form one of the
three distinct ancestral components of modern Europeans, probably later expanded from southeastern Europe. By the
late Mesolithic, coastal foraging societies such as the Ertebølle culture of southern Scandinavia (c. 5,400–3,950 BCE)
counted among the most elaborate hunter-gatherer communities in Europe.
Neolithic and Copper Age
<color=#3366CC>Neolithic Europe</color> emerged in the 7th millennium BC as the first <color=#3366CC>permanent settlements</color> – with houses, <color=#3366CC>wells</color>, granaries,
and defensive structures – appeared in the <color=#3366CC>Balkans</color>. These settlements are linked to Early European Farmers migrating
from <color=#3366CC>Anatolia</color>, the second (after the earlier Mesolithic Western hunter-gatherers) of Europe's three main <color=#3366CC>indigenous</color>
<color=#3366CC>peoples</color>. An archaeological site in the Balkans has the world's oldest securely dated evidence of high-temperature
copper smelting (c. 5000 BC). Solnitsata (c. 4700–4200 BC) – believed to be the oldest urban center in Europe – and
the Varna culture (c. 4550–4100 BC) flourished. Europe's third main indigenous population, the <color=#3366CC>Yamnaya</color> pastoralists,
began expanding into Southeast Europe around 4200 BC but the main <color=#3366CC>Indo-European migration</color> came c. 3300–2600
BC, after which <color=#3366CC>Indo-European languages</color> spread across the continent.
Protohistoric Europe
Bronze Age
The first well-known literate civilization in Europe was the <color=#3366CC>Minoan civilization</color> that arose on the island of <color=#3366CC>Crete</color> and
flourished from approximately the 27th century BC to the 15th century BC.
The Minoans were replaced by the <color=#3366CC>Mycenaean civilization</color> which flourished during the period roughly between 1600
BC, when Helladic culture in mainland Greece was transformed under influences from Minoan Crete, and 1100 BC.
The major Mycenaean cities were <color=#3366CC>Mycenae</color> and Tiryns in Argolis, Pylos in Messenia, <color=#3366CC>Athens</color> in Attica, <color=#3366CC>Thebes</color> and
Orchomenus in Boeotia, and Iolkos in Thessaly. In <color=#3366CC>Crete</color>, the Mycenaeans occupied <color=#3366CC>Knossos</color>. Mycenaean settlement
sites also appeared in Epirus, Macedonia, on islands in the <color=#3366CC>Aegean Sea</color>, on the coast of <color=#3366CC>Asia Minor</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Levant</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Cyprus</color> and Italy. Mycenaean artefacts have been found well outside the limits of the Mycenaean world.
Quite unlike the Minoans, whose society benefited from trade, the Mycenaeans advanced through conquest.
Mycenaean civilization was dominated by a warrior <color=#3366CC>aristocracy</color>. Around 1400 BC, the Mycenaeans extended their
control to Crete, the centre of the Minoan civilization. The Mycenaean civilization perished with the <color=#3366CC>collapse of</color>
<color=#3366CC>Bronze-Age civilization</color> on the eastern shores of the Mediterranean Sea. The collapse has been variously attributed to
Dorian invasion, natural disasters and/or climate change. Whatever the causes, the Mycenaean civilization had
disappeared after LH III C, when the sites of Mycenae and Tiryns were again destroyed. This end, during the last years
of the 12th century BC, occurred after a slow decline of the Mycenaean civilization, which lasted many years before
dying out. The beginning of the 11th century BC opened a new context, that of the protogeometric, the beginning of the
geometric period, the <color=#3366CC>Greek Dark Ages</color> of traditional historiography.
The Bronze Age collapse may be seen in the context of technological history that saw the slow spread of ironworking
technology from present-day <color=#3366CC>Bulgaria</color> and <color=#3366CC>Romania</color> in the 13th and the 12th centuries BC.
The Tumulus culture and the following Urnfield culture of central Europe were part of the origin of the Roman and
<color=#3366CC>Greek</color> cultures.
Iron Age
Classical antiquity
<color=#3366CC>Classical antiquity</color>, also known as the classical era, classical period, classical age, or simply antiquity, is the period
between the 8th century BC and the 5th century AD during which the interwoven civilizations of <color=#3366CC>ancient Greece</color> and
<color=#3366CC>ancient Rome</color>, known together as the Greco-Roman world and centered on the Mediterranean Basin, flourished and
influenced <color=#3366CC>Europe</color>, <color=#3366CC>North Africa</color>, and <color=#3366CC>West Asia</color>.
Ancient Greece
Ancient Greece (also "Hellenic civilisation") was a group of several hundred relatively independent but culturally and

linguistically related city-states ("poleis") – including <color=#3366CC>Athens</color>, Sparta, <color=#3366CC>Thebes</color>, <color=#3366CC>Corinth</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Syracuse</color> – distinguished by

remarkable accomplishments in <color=#3366CC>architecture</color>, <color=#3366CC>philosophy</color>, mathematics, <color=#3366CC>sports</color>, <color=#3366CC>theatre</color> and music. Athens governed
itself with a form of <color=#3366CC>direct democracy</color> and by the late 4th century BC as many as half of the over one thousand existing
Greek cities might have been democracies. Athens was the home of <color=#3366CC>Socrates</color> (c. 470-399 BC), <color=#3366CC>Plato</color> (c. 428–347 BC),
the <color=#3366CC>Platonic Academy</color>, <color=#3366CC>Aristotle</color> (384–322 BC) and the Peripatetic school. The Hellenic city-states established colonies
on the shores of the <color=#3366CC>Black Sea</color> (Greek Crimea and Pontic Greeks) and the Mediterranean Sea (<color=#3366CC>Anatolia</color>, Sicily, and
<color=#3366CC>Southern Italy</color>) and also fought <color=#3366CC>a half century of wars</color> with the <color=#3366CC>Persian Empire</color>.
Hellenic infighting left Greek city states vulnerable, and <color=#3366CC>Philip II of Macedon</color> (r. 359–336 BC) <color=#3366CC>united the Greek city</color>

<color=#3366CC>states under his control</color>. His son, <color=#3366CC>Alexander the Great</color> (r. 336–323 BC), conquered <color=#3366CC>Egypt</color> and <color=#3366CC>Persia</color> and going as far

off as <color=#3366CC>India</color>. During the <color=#3366CC>Hellenistic period</color> (323–30 BC) following the death of Alexander and the <color=#3366CC>wars</color> between <color=#3366CC>his</color>

<color=#3366CC>generals</color>, the resulting <color=#3366CC>Ptolemaic</color>, <color=#3366CC>Seleucid</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Macedonian</color> kingdoms spread Greek culture to regions as far away as
<color=#3366CC>Bactria</color>.
Ancient Rome
Beginning in the 3rd century BC, the <color=#3366CC>Roman Republic</color> began expanding outward from Italy, <color=#3366CC>defeating and absorbing</color>
<color=#3366CC>Hellenistic states</color> and assimilating Greek culture. The most serious challenge to Roman ascent came from the

<color=#3366CC>Phoenician</color> colony of <color=#3366CC>Carthage</color>, and its defeats in the three <color=#3366CC>Punic Wars</color> marked the start of Roman <color=#3366CC>hegemony</color>. First
governed by kings, then as a senatorial republic (the <color=#3366CC>Roman Republic</color>), Rome was transformed into an empire at the
end of the 1st century BC after <color=#3366CC>Julius Caesar</color>'s (r. 49–44 BC) military seizure of power <color=#3366CC>ended republican rule</color>, enabling
<color=#3366CC>Augustus</color> (r. 27 BC-AD 14) and his authoritarian successors. During the reign of the early emperors, Christianity
emerged in the Roman province of Judaea as a movement centered on the 1st-century Jewish preacher and religious
leader <color=#3366CC>Jesus of Nazareth</color> (c. 6 BC-AD 33) and spread through the empire's cities over the following centuries despite
periodic persecution. During the two-century <color=#3366CC>Pax Romana</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Roman Empire</color> became the only state in history to
encircle the entire Mediterranean, spanning three continents from the <color=#3366CC>Atlantic</color> to the <color=#3366CC>Persian Gulf</color>.
In the 3rd century, barbarian invasions and a <color=#3366CC>series of civil wars</color> undermined the Empire. The emperors <color=#3366CC>Diocletian</color> (r.
284–305) and <color=#3366CC>Constantine</color> (r. 306–337) were able to slow down the process of decline by splitting the empire into a
<color=#3366CC>Western</color> part and an <color=#3366CC>Eastern</color> part with the capital in the Greek city of <color=#3366CC>Byzantium</color>, renamed Nova Roma in 330 (marking
the conventional start of the <color=#3366CC>Byzantine Empire</color>) and later as <color=#3366CC>Constantinople</color> ("City of Constantine"). Constantine
declared an official end to state-sponsored persecution of Christians in 313 and convened <color=#3366CC>the council</color> that standardized
the doctrines ("Nicene Christianity") still followed by most Christian churches today. <color=#3366CC>Theodosius I</color> (r. 379–395) made
Nicene Christianity the official religion of the Roman Empire in 381.

The Roman Empire was repeatedly attacked by <color=#3366CC>Hunnic</color>, <color=#3366CC>Germanic</color>, <color=#3366CC>Slavic</color> and other "barbarian" tribes (see: <color=#3366CC>Migration</color>
<color=#3366CC>Period</color>), and in 476 the Western part <color=#3366CC>fell</color> when the <color=#3366CC>last emperor of the Western Roman Empire</color> surrendered to a
<color=#3366CC>barbarian king</color>
Post-classical and medieval Europe
Early Middle Ages
After the <color=#3366CC>fall of Rome</color>, Western Europe fragmented into warring kingdoms that continued to struggle with the
destructive trends of <color=#3366CC>late antiquity</color>: depopulation, deurbanization, and <color=#3366CC>barbarian invasions</color>. As the remnants of Roman
governance disappeared, much of Greco-Roman culture was all but lost in the western part of the old empire. The
gradual adoption of costly <color=#3366CC>parchment</color>, followed by the end of imports of much cheaper <color=#3366CC>papyrus</color>, deepened the
Rome-based Latin Church's monopoly on literacy – already entrenched by the collapse of the municipal schools and
civic offices that rewarded literate civil officials – and left the Church as the primary source of institutional continuity,
legal memory, and administrative expertise for the turbulent post-Roman kingdoms of Western Europe. The Visigoths
and Lombards abandoned <color=#3366CC>Arianism</color> for Nicene Christianity and the <color=#3366CC>pagan</color> Anglo-Saxons, Thuringians, and <color=#3366CC>Bavarians</color>
converted to Christianity between the late 6th and mid-8th centuries but the <color=#3366CC>Umayyad conquest of the Visigothic</color>
<color=#3366CC>Kingdom in Iberia</color> (711–720s) left the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of the Franks</color> ("Francia"), Kingdom of the Lombards (on the <color=#3366CC>Italian</color>
<color=#3366CC>Peninsula</color>) and <color=#3366CC>petty Anglo-Saxon kingdoms</color> (in the <color=#3366CC>British Isles</color>) as the only significant Latin Christian realms. Within
these three realms, however, the cultural influence of the Latin Church - including its <color=#3366CC>prohibitions on cousin marriage</color>,
polygamy, and remarriage within kin groups – ran longest and cut deepest, gradually eroding the extended <color=#3366CC>clans</color> and
<color=#3366CC>kinship</color> groups that had long organized Western European society.
The change in the character of the Constantinople-based <color=#3366CC>Eastern Roman Empire</color> ("Byzantine Empire") was gradual but
by the 7th century Latin titles and usages had been officially replaced with Greek versions. During most of its existence,
the Empire was one of the most powerful economic, cultural, and military forces in Europe and Constantinople was
Europe's largest and wealthiest city. During the period of the Byzantine Papacy (537–752), the <color=#3366CC>bishops of Rome</color>
required Byzantine approval of their elevation, and many bishops were selected from among the apocrisiarii,
ambassadors from the Latin Church to the Byzantine court in Constantinople. The Empire <color=#3366CC>survived plague</color> (541–549)
and a siege of its capital by the Persians and Avars (626), lost <color=#3366CC>Syria</color> (639) and <color=#3366CC>Egypt</color> (642) to the <color=#3366CC>Umayyad Caliphate</color>,
survived <color=#3366CC>another siege this time by the Umayyads</color> (674–678), lost the Balkans (681) to the <color=#3366CC>First Bulgarian Empire</color>, <color=#3366CC>lost</color>
<color=#3366CC>all of North Africa</color> (by 709) to the Umayyads, and then survived a <color=#3366CC>2nd siege by the Umayyads</color> (717 to 718). From the
650s onward, the Mediterranean became a <color=#3366CC>battleground between Arab and Byzantine naval forces</color>, with both sides
launching raids and counterraids against islands and coastal settlements and engaging in a naval arms race. In the
latter part of the <color=#3366CC>Arab–Byzantine wars</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Republic of Venice</color> emerged as an important ally of the Byzantines.
The Latin Church pivoted from the Byzantine Papacy to the Frankish Papacy (756–857) when Pope Stephen II (r.
752–757) became the first bishop of Rome to ever cross the Alps and appealed in person to <color=#3366CC>Frankish leadership</color> for
military aid against the Lombards, resulting in the creation of the Papal States ruled by the bishops of Rome for the
next 1000 years. In 800, <color=#3366CC>Pope Leo III</color> (r. 795–816) crowned <color=#3366CC>Charlemagne</color> (r. 768–814), the King of the Franks, as the
<color=#3366CC>first western "Roman" emperor in over 300 years</color>, a direct provocation to the Byzantines who considered themselves to
be the Roman Empire. After the <color=#3366CC>Christianization of the First Bulgarian Empire</color> (c. 864) and with <color=#3366CC>key support from</color>
<color=#3366CC>Byzantine scholars</color>, the early Cyrillic alphabet, purpose-built for <color=#3366CC>Slavic</color> phonology, was developed there. An increasing
rivalry between the Greek East and Latin West was then expressed in an intense <color=#3366CC>missionary competition</color> among the
Slavs through the 9th and 10th centuries, in which <color=#3366CC>Cyrillic</color> played an important role. While Moravia (c. 863), Bohemia (c.
884), Croatia (by 900), and <color=#3366CC>Poland (966)</color> were drawn into the Latin West, the Serbs (c. 870) and <color=#3366CC>Kievan Rus' (988)</color>
embraced Cyrillic and instead linked themselves with the Greek East.
<color=#3366CC>Charlemagne's empire</color> was partitioned in 843 into <color=#3366CC>West Francia</color>, which developed into the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of France</color>, and
<color=#3366CC>East Francia</color>. The small Anglo-Saxon kingdoms were united into the Kingdom of England in the early 10th century.
East Francia developed into the <color=#3366CC>Holy Roman Empire</color>, conventionally dated from the <color=#3366CC>imperial coronation of Otto the</color>
<color=#3366CC>Great in 962</color>.
From the 8th until the 11th centuries, <color=#3366CC>Muslims</color>, Vikings and <color=#3366CC>Magyars</color> raided and invaded from the south, north, and east
and slavery was a major economic activity. Norse raiders seized captives from the British Isles and from central and
eastern Europe, and from Frankish territories, making Viking-ruled Dublin the largest slave market in Western Europe
and establishing <color=#3366CC>river-based trading routes that linked the Baltic to the Black Sea</color>. The Latin Church spent centuries
attempting to end the enslavement of Christian war captives.
High Middle Ages
The second half of the 11th century saw a rapid and radical transformation in the character of the Latin Church. In 1046
the Holy Roman Emperor <color=#3366CC>Henry III</color> (r. 1046–1056) deposed Pope Gregory VI (r. 1045–1046) – who had purchased the
papacy – along with two other claimants, beginning the process of freeing the papacy from the <color=#3366CC>control of the local</color>
<color=#3366CC>Roman nobility</color>. <color=#3366CC>Pope Leo IX</color> (r. 1049–1054), a German, recruited an international circle of radical reformers who
helped him create an "itinerant papacy" that moved from city to city to hold church councils, consecrate cathedrals, and
negotiate with secular rulers. After centuries of growing rivalry, Leo's dynamic papacy also precipitated the <color=#3366CC>East–West</color>
<color=#3366CC>Schism</color> (also "Great Schism") that split the Latin Church from the <color=#3366CC>Eastern Orthodox Church</color> of the Byzantine Empire in
1054. One of Leo's reformist successors, Pope Nicholas II (r. 1059–1061), and his influential advisor <color=#3366CC>Cardinal</color>
<color=#3366CC>Hildebrand of Sovana</color>, issued the papal bull In nomine Domini (1059), which stripped the Holy Roman Emperor of his
traditional role in appointing popes and established the <color=#3366CC>College of Cardinals</color> as the sole electors. After Cardinal
Hildebrand was himself elected <color=#3366CC>Pope Gregory VII</color> (r. 1073–1085), he worked both to improve the moral integrity and
independence of Church clergy and to establish the total freedom of the Church from secular interference ("libertas
ecclesiae"). By challenging the Holy Roman Emperor <color=#3366CC>Henry IV</color>'s (r. 1084–1105) right to appoint church officials,
Gregory began the <color=#3366CC>Investiture Controversy</color>, a struggle for supremacy between the Church and the secular monarchies
of Europe.
In 1095 the Byzantine emperor requested military support in his <color=#3366CC>Empire's conflict with the Seljuk Empire</color>. In response,
<color=#3366CC>Pope Urban II</color> (r. 1088–1099) spread a <color=#3366CC>message of holy war</color> across Europe. The ensuing <color=#3366CC>Crusades</color> led to the
foundation of <color=#3366CC>small Catholic states</color> in the <color=#3366CC>Levant</color>, which lasted for two centuries until their final outpost, Acre, <color=#3366CC>fell</color> to the
<color=#3366CC>Mamluk Sultanate</color>. Even as the later Crusades were failing, however, <color=#3366CC>Iberian Christian attacks</color> on Muslim-ruled
<color=#3366CC>al-Andalus</color> were reversing the 8th century <color=#3366CC>Muslim conquest</color> of the <color=#3366CC>Visigothic Kingdom</color>. Further expanding the Latin
West, Scandinavians (Denmark, Norway and Sweden) <color=#3366CC>converted to Latin Christianity</color>.

Along with the existing <color=#3366CC>Republic of Venice</color>, new Italian <color=#3366CC>city-state maritime republics</color> like <color=#3366CC>Genoa</color> and <color=#3366CC>Pisa</color> (from c. 1000),
and <color=#3366CC>Florence</color> (from 1115), thrived on expanding trade, led a commercial revolution, and made Italy the most productive
region of Europe in the Middle Ages. <color=#3366CC>Pope Alexander III</color> (r. 1159–1181) strongly backed the <color=#3366CC>1167–1168 alliance of</color>
<color=#3366CC>these northern Italian cities</color>, which defeated the Holy Roman Empire at the Battle of Legnano (1176) and won their
effective independence from the Empire in the Peace of Constance (1183). After capturing the son of the Holy Roman
Emperor at the Battle of Fossalta (1249), <color=#3366CC>Bologna</color>’s Liber Paradisus purchased the freedom of nearly 6,000 serfs in
1256, the first abolition of serfdom in Europe. Florence passed laws in the 1290s to align itself <color=#3366CC>with the Catholic Church</color>
<color=#3366CC>against the Empire</color> and ensure that the city's merchant and artisan guilds controlled the government.
As medieval Europe became perhaps the first society in human history to build an economy on nonhuman power, land
under cultivation and the number of towns grew together in northern and central Europe. Central Europe alone saw
some three thousand new towns founded between the eleventh and early fourteenth centuries. By 1250, robust
population increase had brought the economy to levels it would not see again in some areas until the 19th century.
Beginning in the 13th century, the <color=#3366CC>Hanseatic League</color>, a commercial and defensive network of merchant guilds and
market towns in <color=#3366CC>Central</color> and <color=#3366CC>Northern Europe</color>, grew to dominate maritime trade in the Baltic and North seas in the
following century. Medieval engineers produced the first <color=#3366CC>weight-driven mechanical clocks</color> by the end of the 13th century
and every city in Europe soon possessed at least one. Historical demographers estimate that sustained growth during
the High Middle Ages – enabled by a thriving north-south "bipolar urban network" - pushed Europe's population beyond
the peak levels reached during the era of the Roman Empire.
In northern Italy at the turn of the 13th century, Leonardo da Pisa (c. 1170-c. 1240-50) - commonly known as <color=#3366CC>Fibonacci</color>
- popularized <color=#3366CC>Arabic numerals</color> and <color=#3366CC>base-10 positional notation</color>, while the <color=#3366CC>University of Bologna</color>, the oldest university
currently in continuous operation in the world, was being established. Two more universities were established in the

early 13th century in <color=#3366CC>France</color> (the <color=#3366CC>University of Paris</color>) and <color=#3366CC>England</color> (the <color=#3366CC>University of Oxford</color>). These new institutions
were a foundation for many of Europe's future achievements, especially in science. Initially, they were key participants
in the <color=#3366CC>rediscovery of the works of Aristotle</color>, which led the Italian priest <color=#3366CC>Thomas Aquinas</color> (1225–1274) and other thinkers
to develop the philosophy of <color=#3366CC>scholasticism</color>.
After conquering the fractured principalities of the former Kievan Rus' and the <color=#3366CC>Kipchak-Cuman Confederation</color>, Mongol
armies <color=#3366CC>invaded Central Europe</color> in 1241, defeating a Polish-Moravian force at Legnica and crushing the <color=#3366CC>Hungarians</color> at
Mohi before <color=#3366CC>withdrawing</color>. The conquered regions were later known as the <color=#3366CC>Golden Horde</color>. The adjacent Russian
principalities had a vassalage relationship with the Khanate for the next 200 years.
Late Middle Ages
Centuries of European prosperity and growth unraveled during the <color=#3366CC>crisis of the late Middle Ages</color>. The Great Famine of
1315–1317 caused extreme levels of crime, disease, mass death, and even <color=#3366CC>cannibalism</color> and <color=#3366CC>infanticide</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Black</color>
<color=#3366CC>Death</color> (1346–1353) killed people in a matter of days, reducing the population of some areas by half as many survivors
fled: The Black Death touched every aspect of life, hastening a process of social, economic, and cultural transformation
already underway.... Fields were abandoned, workplaces stood idle, international trade was suspended. Traditional
bonds of kinship, village, and even religion were broken amid the horrors of death, flight, and failed expectations.
"People cared no more for dead men than we care for dead goats," wrote one survivor.
Popular uprisings, including the Jacquerie (1358) and the <color=#3366CC>Peasants' Revolt</color> (1381), shook both France and England,
while the prestige and unity of the Catholic Church suffered long-term damage from the <color=#3366CC>Avignon Papacy</color> (1309–1376)
and the <color=#3366CC>Western Schism</color> (1378–1417).
Despite these crises, a great effort to rediscover and revive the cultural achievements of <color=#3366CC>classical antiquity</color> began in

14th-century Florence, spread <color=#3366CC>across Italy</color> and Europe, and transformed <color=#3366CC>art</color>, <color=#3366CC>architecture</color>, and <color=#3366CC>literature</color>. Renaissance
humanists, including several 15th- and 16th-century popes, perceived their repossession of a lost past as a <color=#3366CC>rebirth</color> of
civilization.
The Byzantine Empire - the last remnant of the Roman Empire - <color=#3366CC>fell in 1453</color> when <color=#3366CC>massive cannons</color> of the <color=#3366CC>Ottoman</color>
<color=#3366CC>Empire</color> finally breached the walls of Constantinople, ending eleven centuries of Byzantine civilization in Eastern
Europe.
Early modern Europe
Early modern Europe spans the centuries between the <color=#3366CC>Middle Ages</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Industrial Revolution</color>. The period includes

the <color=#3366CC>rapid spread of mechanical movable-type printing</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Age of Discovery</color>, the Protestant <color=#3366CC>Reformation</color>, the <color=#3366CC>European</color>

<color=#3366CC>colonisation of the Americas</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Scientific Revolution</color>, the disastrous <color=#3366CC>Thirty Years' War</color> and the emergence of the <color=#3366CC>five</color>
<color=#3366CC>great European powers</color>.
Printing
From a single location in the Free Imperial City of Mainz around 1440, <color=#3366CC>printing had spread</color> to about 270 cities across
Europe and produced more than 20 million volumes by the end of the 15th century. Just 25 miles away, the Frankfurt
Book Fair was established by 1462 and remained the primary marketplace for printers and publishers and the center of
Europe's book trade for the next two hundred years. By the 16th century, the manuscript culture of the Middle Ages,
where <color=#3366CC>facts</color> were few and far between, had begun to give way to a printing culture where living scholars could compare
their own observations with those of other (living) scholars, transforming how <color=#3366CC>knowledge was created, preserved and</color>
<color=#3366CC>disseminated</color>.
Exploration, epidemics and colonies
Following explorations of the coast of Africa using <color=#3366CC>new ship technology</color> led by the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Portugal</color>’s <color=#3366CC>Prince Henry</color>
<color=#3366CC>the Navigator</color> (1394–1460) seeking an eastern maritime route to India and <color=#3366CC>Spanish-funded voyages to the West</color>, the
two nations signed the <color=#3366CC>Treaty of Tordesillas</color> (1494), granting Africa and the East to Portugal while Spain claimed the
Atlantic and everything beyond it. The Portuguese explorer <color=#3366CC>Vasco da Gama</color> (c. 1460s-1524) completed the first
recorded trip directly from Europe to the Indian subcontinent (1497–1499). The Florentine <color=#3366CC>Amerigo Vespucci</color>'s <color=#3366CC>Mundus</color>
<color=#3366CC>Novus</color> letter, published in 1503 and repeatedly reprinted, provided the first explicit articulation in print that the lands
discovered by European navigators to the West were not the edges of Asia, but rather an <color=#3366CC>entirely different continent</color> (a
"New World"). Between 1519 and 1522, the <color=#3366CC>Magellan–Elcano expedition</color> achieved the first circumnavigation of Earth in
history, including the first crossing of the Pacific by a European expedition, revealing the vast scale of that ocean. The
encounter with continents that were completely unknown to the <color=#3366CC>ancients</color> had a profound impact on European
intellectual life and specifically undermined the authority of <color=#3366CC>Claudius Ptolemy</color>, the 2nd-century <color=#3366CC>Alexandrian</color> scholar
whose <color=#3366CC>geographic</color> and <color=#3366CC>astronomical</color> models had long been considered infallible.
Portugal forged the <color=#3366CC>first global empire</color>, but by the late 16th century, the Hispanic Monarchy (incorporating Portugal from
1580 to 1640) had become the world's largest empire, with silver from its American colonies accounting for at least
twenty percent of its total revenue. Epidemics of smallpox and other Eurasian diseases swept the Americas
subsequent to European contact, killing between 10 million and 100 million people, up to 95% of the indigenous
population of the Americas. While Spain dominated the Americas and controlled the Philippines, in the 17th and 18th
centuries Spanish dominance was challenged by the <color=#3366CC>Netherlands</color>, <color=#3366CC>France</color> and <color=#3366CC>Britain</color>. With a plantation economy
fueled by slave labor, Saint-Domingue – the "<color=#3366CC>Pearl of the Antilles</color>" – was the richest colony in the 18th-century <color=#3366CC>French</color>
<color=#3366CC>empire</color>. Europe's colonial plantation economies were sustained by the <color=#3366CC>Atlantic slave trade</color>, which forcibly transported
12 million enslaved Africans to the Americas between the 16th and 19th centuries.
The diffusion of New World crops during the <color=#3366CC>Columbian exchange</color> reshaped Europe. <color=#3366CC>Maize</color> arrived first and spread
swiftly through the Mediterranean and Balkans in the 16th century while the <color=#3366CC>potato</color> spread far more slowly in northern
Europe. The higher and more reliable caloric yield per acre of both crops altered the <color=#3366CC>peasant</color> diet and contributed to the
retreat of recurrent famine and to European population growth and urbanization.
Reformation
Sparked by the German priest <color=#3366CC>Martin Luther</color>’s (1483–1546) <color=#3366CC>Ninety-five Theses</color> (1517) and spread by the new <color=#3366CC>movable</color>
<color=#3366CC>type</color> <color=#3366CC>printing press</color> in vernacular languages (i.e. not Latin), the <color=#3366CC>Protestant Reformation</color> was a religious and political
challenge to the Catholic Church. In 1527, mutinous troops of the <color=#3366CC>Habsburg</color> Holy Roman Emperor <color=#3366CC>Charles V</color> (r.
1519-1556) – many of them fervent Protestant converts – sacked Rome, imprisoned Pope Clement VII (r. 1523–1534),
humiliated the Church, and decimated Rome’s population, which plummeted from over 55,000 to barely 10,000 through
a combination of massacre, starvation, and plague. As the movement branched into <color=#3366CC>Lutheranism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Calvinism</color>, and
<color=#3366CC>Anglicanism</color>, it triggered the Catholic <color=#3366CC>Counter-Reformation</color>, reshaped Europe’s political landscape and exploded into
nearly <color=#3366CC>two centuries of religious wars</color>. States were also torn apart internally by religious strife fostered by their external
enemies, a fate suffered by France <color=#3366CC>between 1562 and 1598</color>.
During the <color=#3366CC>Thirty Years' War</color> (1618–1648), entire regions of the German states and, to a lesser extent, the <color=#3366CC>Low</color>
<color=#3366CC>Countries</color>, the Crown of Bohemia and northern parts of Italy were scavenged bare by foraging armies, causing
widespread famine, while bankrupting many of the states involved. Between one-fourth and one-third of the German
population perished from direct military causes or from disease and starvation as <color=#3366CC>social order disintegrated</color>. Between 4
and 8 million people died due to the war, the vast majority being civilians, making it the most devastating European
conflict until the 20th century. The <color=#3366CC>Peace of Westphalia</color> ending the war guaranteed the right to practice <color=#3366CC>Catholicism</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Lutheranism</color> and <color=#3366CC>Calvinism</color> as well as the independence of the religiously tolerant Dutch Republic, which established a
<color=#3366CC>safe haven for European Jews</color>.
Scientific Revolution
Italian <color=#3366CC>astronomer</color> <color=#3366CC>Galileo Galilei</color>’s (1564–1642) <color=#3366CC>early 17th-century telescopic observations</color> began the transformation of
what had been a narrowly technical revision of <color=#3366CC>classical astronomy</color> into an increasingly aggressive challenge to
traditional cosmology and its long-standing synthesis with Christian theology. English <color=#3366CC>mathematical physicist</color> <color=#3366CC>Isaac</color>
<color=#3366CC>Newton</color>’s (1643–1727) <color=#3366CC>Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica</color> (1687) dissolved the ancient boundary between
the celestial and the terrestrial by showing how a single mathematical law – the <color=#3366CC>law of universal gravitation</color> – ruled both
realms, the first great unification of physics.
The upheaval of the Scientific Revolution ended the medieval view of <color=#3366CC>natural philosophy</color> as the servant (or
"handmaiden") of theology. As natural philosophy continued to grow in power, self-confidence and independence
during the 17th century, the intellectual attitude of educated people shifted from fides quaerens intellectum toward a
mode of understanding increasingly detached from religion. The "New Science" that emerged by the end of the century
broke sharply with the natural philosophy that had preceded it, departed from previous Greek conceptions and
traditions, was more mechanistic in its worldview and more integrated with mathematics, and was obsessed with the
acquisition and interpretation of new evidence.
Great powers
During the 1640s and 1650s, England endured <color=#3366CC>civil war</color> (1642–1651), the <color=#3366CC>Spanish Empire</color> fractured from simultaneous
revolts in Portugal (1640–1668) and Catalonia (1640–1659), and the <color=#3366CC>Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth</color> faced
near-extinction from a Cossack rebellion (1648–1657), the <color=#3366CC>Polish–Russian War (1654–1667)</color> and <color=#3366CC>Swedish invasion</color>
(1655–1660). The failure of the Ottoman Empire's <color=#3366CC>second and last attempt to capture the Habsburg capital of Vienna</color>
<color=#3366CC>(1683)</color> resulted in the loss of Hungary to the Habsburgs (1699) and marked the end of the <color=#3366CC>empire's expansion into</color>
<color=#3366CC>Europe</color>.
Largely spared from the devastation of the Thirty Years' War, <color=#3366CC>France</color> was the <color=#3366CC>leading European power at the end of the</color>
<color=#3366CC>17th century</color>. England, however, had surpassed Italy to have the most productive economy in the world and the
<color=#3366CC>Glorious Revolution</color> (1688) - which subjected the English crown to Parliament – sparked a Financial Revolution that
made the country into a more creditworthy borrower than its absolutist rivals on the Continent whose unchecked
monarchs were considered poorer credit risks by lenders. These economic and financial advantages over France were
tested in the <color=#3366CC>War of the Spanish Succession</color> (1701–1714), in which a pan-European coalition united to oppose France,
Britain won the strategic ports of <color=#3366CC>Gibraltar</color> and <color=#3366CC>Minorca</color>, and the country was set on a course towards "maritime,
commercial, and financial supremacy."
The decline of the previously powerful Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, Ottoman Empire and <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Sweden</color>
was mirrored by the ascent of three centralized, absolutist monarchies: the <color=#3366CC>Habsburg monarchy</color> ("Austria"), the
<color=#3366CC>Tsardom of Russia</color> and Brandenburg–Prussia. Following the administrative and military models of France's <color=#3366CC>Louis XIV</color>
the "Sun King" (r. 1643–1715), these states built the strong armies and large bureaucracies that the <color=#3366CC>escalating costs of</color>
<color=#3366CC>gunpowder warfare</color> demanded and expanded at the expense of their neighbors. Sweden yielded territory to Russia and
the Tsar of Russia became Emperor <color=#3366CC>Peter the Great</color> (r. Russia 1682–1725) of the Russian Empire in 1721 while
<color=#3366CC>Catherine the Great</color>'s (r. 1762–1796) reforms caused the Empire to develop into a major European power. <color=#3366CC>Frederick</color>
<color=#3366CC>the Great</color> (r. Prussia 1740–1786) improved the Prussian army and took Silesia from Austria (1740–1742). Finally, the
Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth <color=#3366CC>was carved up between the three rising powers</color> (1772–1795).
The five great powers of Europe that emerged in the 18th century – Austria, France, Prussia, Russia, and the United
Kingdom – formed the <color=#3366CC>Concert of Europe</color> that dominated European politics in the 19th century and up to World War I.
Enlightenment
The <color=#3366CC>Age of Enlightenment</color> (also "Age of Reason" or simply "the Enlightenment") was a period of <color=#3366CC>intellectual</color> and cultural
flourishing that emerged in the late 17th century in <color=#3366CC>Western Europe</color> and reached its peak in the 18th century as its
ideas spread more widely across Europe. Characterized by an emphasis on <color=#3366CC>reason</color>, empirical evidence, and the

<color=#3366CC>scientific method</color>, the Enlightenment promoted ideals of <color=#3366CC>individual liberty</color>, religious tolerance, <color=#3366CC>progress</color>, and <color=#3366CC>natural</color>
<color=#3366CC>rights</color>. Its thinkers advocated for <color=#3366CC>constitutional government</color>, the <color=#3366CC>separation of church and state</color>, and the application of
rational principles to social and political reform. The movement was characterized by the widespread circulation of
ideas through new institutions: <color=#3366CC>scientific academies</color>, literary salons, <color=#3366CC>coffeehouses</color>, <color=#3366CC>Masonic lodges</color>, and an expanding
print culture of <color=#3366CC>books</color>, <color=#3366CC>journals</color>, and pamphlets. The ideas of the Enlightenment undermined the authority of the
<color=#3366CC>monarchy</color> and religious officials and paved the way for the political <color=#3366CC>revolutions</color> of the 18th and 19th centuries. A variety
of 19th-century movements, including <color=#3366CC>liberalism</color>, <color=#3366CC>socialism</color>, and <color=#3366CC>neoclassicism</color>, trace their intellectual heritage to the
Enlightenment.
Industrial Revolution
The <color=#3366CC>Industrial Revolution</color> was the most significant transition in human civilization since the <color=#3366CC>Agricultural Revolution</color>. It
was the first breakthrough from an agrarian, handicraft economy to one dominated by industry and machine
manufacture, initiating unprecedented, cumulative and self-sustaining advances in technology and economic
productivity during which Western Europe emerged as the world's most powerful civilization, <color=#3366CC>eclipsing all of its Eurasian</color>
<color=#3366CC>rivals</color>.
Originating in Britain in the mid-18th century with the mechanisation of textile manufacturing, advancements in
iron-making and increased use of coal, it subsequently spread to Western Europe. Technological advancements, most
notably the steam engine, accelerated and sustained the industrialisation process. Trade expansion was enabled by
the introduction of <color=#3366CC>canals</color>, improved roads, and railways. The introduction of <color=#3366CC>steam power</color> (fuelled primarily by coal)
and powered machinery (mainly in <color=#3366CC>textile manufacturing</color>) underpinned the dramatic increases in production capacity.
The development of all-metal <color=#3366CC>machine tools</color> in the first two decades of the 19th century facilitated the manufacture of
more production machines for manufacturing in other industries. The effects spread throughout Western Europe and
North America during the 19th century, eventually affecting most of the world.
The Industrial Revolution was the first time population and per-person income rose simultaneously. Europe's population
increased from 100 million in 1700 to 400 million by 1900.
Long 19th century
During the "long 19th century" (1789–1914), Europe was transformed by the <color=#3366CC>Industrial Revolution</color> and by the political

upheavals of the <color=#3366CC>French Revolution</color>, <color=#3366CC>Napoleonic Wars</color>, the <color=#3366CC>rise of nationalism</color>, the <color=#3366CC>revolutions of 1848</color> and <color=#3366CC>German</color>
<color=#3366CC>unification</color>.
French Revolution
The <color=#3366CC>French Revolution</color> was a decade of political and social upheaval in France and Europe at the end of the 18th
century. After France's costly intervention in the <color=#3366CC>American Revolutionary War</color> and <color=#3366CC>repeated failed attempts</color>, in 1789
<color=#3366CC>King Louis XVI</color> (r. 1774–1792) summoned the Estates-General – a representative body comprising the medieval

"estates" of <color=#3366CC>clergy</color>, <color=#3366CC>nobility</color> and <color=#3366CC>commoners</color> – to help solve France's fiscal crisis. The <color=#3366CC>Third Estate</color>, joined by some
members of the other two, declared itself a National Assembly. After the <color=#3366CC>storming of the Bastille on 14 July</color>, the
Assembly passed the <color=#3366CC>Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen</color>, abolished feudalism, sought complete control
over the Catholic Church in France, banned guilds and approved France's first written constitution, briefly turning
France into a constitutional monarchy. The French Revolutionary Army's unexpected victory over an Austro-Prussian
invasion emboldened the newly assembled National Convention to abolish the monarchy and make France a republic
in 1792. The Convention created the Committee of Public Safety and mandated national <color=#3366CC>conscription</color> (the levée en
masse) in 1793, and abolished colonial slavery in 1794.
Following the French general <color=#3366CC>Napoleon Bonaparte</color>’s 1796 invasion of Italy and the 1798 French invasion of
Switzerland, a network of satellite states replaced previous regimes. In 1799 during the War of the Second Coalition,
Napoleon abandoned a French army in Egypt, returned to Paris, <color=#3366CC>overthrew the leadership</color> of the Republic and then

crowned himself <color=#3366CC>Emperor</color> in 1804. Despite crushing victories at <color=#3366CC>Austerlitz</color> (1805) and <color=#3366CC>Jena</color> (1806) ending both the <color=#3366CC>third</color>
and <color=#3366CC>fourth</color> coalitions, however, his empire later collapsed following an <color=#3366CC>invasion of Russia</color>, a disastrous retreat from
Moscow (1812) and a decisive defeat at <color=#3366CC>Leipzig</color> (1813).
French politics were permanently polarized after the Revolution – new names were given, "left" and "right", for the
supporters and opponents of the principles of the Revolution. French-controlled areas abolished feudal privileges and
seigneurial dues, liberalised <color=#3366CC>property laws</color>, ended the guilds of merchants and craftsmen to facilitate <color=#3366CC>entrepreneurship</color>,
reduced trade barriers, legalised divorce, closed the <color=#3366CC>Jewish ghettos</color> and emancipated Jewish populations, and
introduced the metric system. Italy and Switzerland both experienced radical change but Germany was also deeply
impacted by the dissolution of the thousand-year-old Holy Roman Empire. Its replacement by the <color=#3366CC>Confederation of the</color>
<color=#3366CC>Rhine</color> fueled German nationalism, with far-reaching consequences.
Concert of Europe
At the <color=#3366CC>Congress of Vienna</color> (1814–1815), the great European powers agreed to massive territorial changes in Central
and Eastern Europe and to <color=#3366CC>maintain a European balance of power</color>, initially intended to be managed with regular
meetings between them (the "<color=#3366CC>Congress System</color>").
Beginning with uprisings in Sicily and <color=#3366CC>France</color>, the <color=#3366CC>revolutions of 1848</color> became the most widespread revolutionary wave
in European history. In Paris, street fighting forced the <color=#3366CC>abdication of the king</color> and the proclamation of the French
Second Republic (1848–1852), a fast collapse of a great power monarchy that emboldened both liberals and
nationalists and encouraged demands for both constitutions and <color=#3366CC>nation states</color>. While <color=#3366CC>Denmark transitioned peacefully</color>
<color=#3366CC>to a constitutional monarchy</color> and Sardinia-Piedmont secured the Statuto Albertino (later the constitution of a united
Italy), conservative reaction triumphed almost everywhere else. In France, the Second Republic curdled into
authoritarian rule and then the Second French Empire (1852–1870). Most consequentially, the <color=#3366CC>King of Prussia's</color>
<color=#3366CC>rejection of the crown of a "German Empire"</color> offered by the Frankfurt National Assembly – the first freely elected
parliament for all German states – suggested to Germans that parliamentary liberalism was incapable of achieving a
German nation state, a lesson with far-reaching consequences for Europe.
Governments increasingly took control of both education and marriage away from churches, abolished taxes and tithes
for the support of <color=#3366CC>established religions</color>, and excluded bishops from legislative bodies. In France, hostility to the Catholic
Church became a major issue and in Germany in the 1870s there was a fierce Kulturkampf (culture war) against
Catholics. Notwithstanding these conflicts and tensions, however, the last decades of the long 19th century –
sometimes known as the <color=#3366CC>Belle Époque</color> (1871–1914) – were characterised by unusual political stability in <color=#3366CC>Western</color> and
<color=#3366CC>Central Europe</color>. With the notable exception of Russia, all of Europe's major powers had become <color=#3366CC>constitutional</color>
<color=#3366CC>monarchies</color> or republics. An upper-class gentleman could travel through much of Western Europe without a <color=#3366CC>passport</color>
and even reside abroad with minimal bureaucratic regulation. For many Europeans, transnational, class-based
affiliations were as important as national identities, particularly among aristocrats.
The <color=#3366CC>Franco-Prussian War</color> (1871) that ended a French empire and created a German one also left behind an enmity
between France and Germany because of the loss of Alsace-Lorraine. The new <color=#3366CC>German Empire</color> (1871–1918)
industrialised rapidly and <color=#3366CC>sought to overtake Britain</color> to become Europe's leading industrial power. In 1882, <color=#3366CC>Otto von</color>
<color=#3366CC>Bismarck</color>, the architect of the <color=#3366CC>unification of Germany</color> and chancellor of the Empire, drove the creation of the Triple
Alliance, a military alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy. In 1907, France, Russia and Britain formed the
Triple Entente.
Nationalism
The most revolutionary political force in 19th-century Europe was <color=#3366CC>nationalism</color>, which emerged initially among the <color=#3366CC>South</color>
<color=#3366CC>Slavs</color> and Greeks in the multi-ethnic Ottoman Empire. The success of the anti-Ottoman Serbian Revolution
(1804–1817) was followed by the <color=#3366CC>Greek War of Independence</color> (1821–1829), which became a cause for European
'philhellenes' who viewed the Greek conflict as a civilizational battle to free the Greek "cradle of Europe" from a foreign
occupier. Closer to the heartland of the Empire, the anti-Ottoman Bulgarian insurrection of 1876, and the
<color=#3366CC>Russo-Turkish War</color> (1877–1878) that followed led to the re-establishment of Bulgaria in 1878.
The <color=#3366CC>Austro-Hungarian Empire</color> had the advantage of size and a large army but rising nationalism acted as a powerful
centrifugal force that strained the multi-ethnic fabric of the Empire, fostering internal dissent and demands for
self-determination that progressively undermined the stability of <color=#3366CC>Habsburg</color> rule. In the <color=#3366CC>Hungarian Revolution of 1848</color>,
Hungarian nationalists battled Austria only finally losing when <color=#3366CC>Russia sent some 200,000 troops to restore Habsburg</color>
<color=#3366CC>rule</color>. Russia also crushed large nationalist revolts in Congress Poland in 1830 and 1863–64 and attempted to "Russify"
Polish language, culture and religion.
French conquests of smaller German and Italian states during the Napoleonic Wars encouraged 19th century demands
for national unity. <color=#3366CC>Italian unification</color> (also known as the "Risorgimento") was the <color=#3366CC>consolidation of the seven states of the</color>
<color=#3366CC>Italian Peninsula</color> into the Kingdom of Italy in the 1860s, culminating with the end of the Papal States in 1870. Von
Bismarck, the Minister President of Prussia in the 1860s leveraged German nationalism and a series of short, decisive
wars – including the <color=#3366CC>Franco-Prussian War</color>, which toppled the Second French Empire – to <color=#3366CC>consolidate dozens of</color>
<color=#3366CC>German states</color> into the powerful German Empire in 1871.
Under the influence of Spanish nationalism, Spain's 18th century Castilian-centric assimilation policies towards

Catalan-speaking territories (<color=#3366CC>Catalonia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Valencia</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Balearic Islands</color>, part of <color=#3366CC>Aragon</color>) and other national minorities
accelerated in the 19th century.
Nationalism stimulated the emergence of <color=#3366CC>national educational systems</color> that prioritized the study of national heritage,
national language, and patriotic identity over historical accuracy. <color=#3366CC>Compulsory elementary education</color> became standard
in Germany and then across Western Europe and then was extended to girls. By the 1890s, strong movements
emerged in some countries, including France and Germany, to extend compulsory education to the secondary level.
Emigration
Pushed by both poverty and the displacement of peasant farming and artisan manufacturing, 20% of Europe's rapidly
growing population – 65 million people – emigrated between 1815 and 1939, primarily to the United States, Argentina,
Canada and Brazil:
Second Industrial Revolution
The <color=#3366CC>Second Industrial Revolution</color> was a phase of rapid scientific discovery, <color=#3366CC>standardization</color>, <color=#3366CC>mass production</color> and
industrialisation that is generally dated between 1870 and 1914.
Although poverty remained pervasive, living standards for lower-class Europeans rose steadily as the century
progressed. Wages increased, housing and diets improved, and working hours fell.
New Imperialism
The <color=#3366CC>Scramble for Africa</color> was the colonisation of Africa from the mid-1870s to World War I by seven Western European

powers (Belgium, <color=#3366CC>France</color>, <color=#3366CC>Germany</color>, <color=#3366CC>Italy</color>, <color=#3366CC>Portugal</color>, <color=#3366CC>Spain</color> and the <color=#3366CC>United Kingdom</color>) enabled by new technologies
including steamships, railways and telegraphs. The United Kingdom combined <color=#3366CC>naval supremacy</color> and economic and
other influence to build a <color=#3366CC>global empire</color> – the largest empire in human history (comprising more than 25% of all land on
the planet in 1920) – on which "the sun never set".
World wars
World War I
At the beginning of the 20th century two rival alliances of European great powers – the Triple Alliance of the German
Empire, Austro-Hungarian Monarchy and Kingdom of Italy and the Triple Entente of the French Republic, Russian
Empire and United Kingdom (Great Britain) – opposed each other and were committed to come to the aid of their
alliance partners. In 1914, Austria-Hungary threatened the Kingdom of Serbia. In response, Russia mobilized to
threaten Austria. Germany then mobilized to threaten Russia and preemptively strike France through Belgium while
Britain declared war after Germany violated Belgian neutrality.
Modern armies with <color=#3366CC>machine guns</color> and massive artillery fought indecisively for 3 years from <color=#3366CC>fortified and static trenches</color>
on the <color=#3366CC>Western Front</color>. Single battles like <color=#3366CC>Verdun</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Somme</color> killed hundreds of thousands. Russia collapsed in the
<color=#3366CC>February Revolution</color> of 1917 and Germany claimed victory on the <color=#3366CC>Eastern Front</color>. The <color=#3366CC>October Revolution</color> brought the
<color=#3366CC>Bolsheviks</color> to power, leading to the creation of the <color=#3366CC>Soviet Union</color>. With American entry into the war in 1917, and the
failure of <color=#3366CC>Germany's spring 1918 offensive</color>, Germany had run out of manpower. Germany's allies, Austria-Hungary and
the Ottoman Empire, surrendered and dissolved, followed by Germany. Over 65 million European soldiers were
mobilised from 1914 to 1918; 20 million soldiers and civilians died.
The world war was settled by the victors at the <color=#3366CC>Paris Peace Conference, 1919</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Treaty of Versailles</color> significantly
reduced Germany's military power and required the nation to accept responsibility for the conflict and pay extensive
financial reparations. The conference also created the <color=#3366CC>League of Nations</color> and transferred <color=#3366CC>German</color> and <color=#3366CC>Ottoman</color>
territories to the control of Allied powers, chiefly Britain and France, as "mandates". The collapse of the Russian Empire
in the First World War enabled the major powers to reestablish an independent Second Polish Republic, which survived
until 1939, as well as an independent Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Estonia and, briefly, independent Ukraine, Armenia,
Georgia, and Azerbaijan. Independent nations of <color=#3366CC>Czechoslovakia</color>, Hungary and Yugoslavia were also created in central
Europe from the defunct Austro-Hungarian and German empires. Multiple nations were required to sign minority rights
treaties.
Interwar period
The Allied victory in the First World War seemed to mark the triumph of <color=#3366CC>liberalism</color>. As early as 1917, however, the
emerging liberal order was being challenged by the new <color=#3366CC>communist movement</color>. Communist revolts were beaten back
everywhere else, but succeeded in Russia. During the 1920s, Italy's democratic institutions were dismantled and it
became a totalitarian state.
After the <color=#3366CC>Wall Street crash of 1929</color>, most of the world sank into a Great Depression; prices and profits fell and
unemployment soared. The worst hit sectors included heavy industry, export-oriented agriculture, mining and
lumbering, and construction. World trade fell by two-thirds.
Authoritarian regimes ended democracies in the 1920s and 1930s in <color=#3366CC>Portugal</color>, Lithuania, Poland, Austria and Greece.
A German <color=#3366CC>fascist party</color> began to transform Germany into a totalitarian state in 1933 and allied with the <color=#3366CC>Empire of Japan</color>
in the Anti-Comintern Pact in 1936. The League of Nations failed to resolve any major crises and by 1937 it was largely
ignored. Supported by <color=#3366CC>Nazi Germany</color> and Fascist Italy, <color=#3366CC>Nationalist rebels</color> overthrew the Second Spanish Republic in
the <color=#3366CC>Spanish Civil War</color> (1936–1939). With <color=#3366CC>acquiescence from Britain and France</color>, Nazi Germany annexed part of
Czechoslovakia in 1938, and then occupied the rest of Czechoslovakia, signed the "Pact of Steel" alliance with Fascist
Italy and made a <color=#3366CC>non-aggression treaty</color> with the Soviet Union in 1939. By 1940, there were only four <color=#3366CC>liberal</color>
<color=#3366CC>democracies</color> left on the European continent: France, Finland, Switzerland and Sweden.
World War II
The German Führer <color=#3366CC>Adolf Hitler</color> launched the <color=#3366CC>Second World War</color> with invasions of <color=#3366CC>Poland</color> (1939), Denmark (1940),
Norway (1940), the Netherlands (1940), and <color=#3366CC>France</color> (1940). Britain defeated Germany's air attacks in the <color=#3366CC>Battle of</color>
<color=#3366CC>Britain</color> (1940). The <color=#3366CC>invasion of the Soviet Union</color> began in June 1941. The German <color=#3366CC>Wehrmacht</color> was stopped close to
Moscow in December 1941.
Over the next year the Germans started to suffer a series of defeats. War raged between the <color=#3366CC>Axis Powers</color> (Nazi
Germany, Fascist Italy, and the Empire of Japan) and the <color=#3366CC>Allied Forces</color> (British Empire, Soviet Union, and the United
States). The Allied Forces won in North Africa, invaded Italy in 1943, and liberated France in 1944. In 1945 Germany
itself was invaded from the east by the Soviet Union and <color=#3366CC>from the west by the other Allies</color>. The Soviet <color=#3366CC>Red Army</color>
conquered the <color=#3366CC>Reichstag</color> in the <color=#3366CC>Battle of Berlin</color> and Germany surrendered.
World War II was the deadliest conflict in human history, causing <color=#3366CC>between 60 and 75 million deaths</color>, the majority of
whom were civilians (approximately 38 to 55 million). The period was also marked by systematic genocide. In
1942–1945, separately from the war-related deaths, the <color=#3366CC>Nazis</color> killed over 11 million civilians identified through
IBM-enabled censuses, including the <color=#3366CC>majority of the Jews</color> and <color=#3366CC>Gypsies</color> of Europe, millions of Polish and <color=#3366CC>Soviet</color> Slavs,
homosexuals, Jehovah's Witnesses, disabled people, and political enemies. Meanwhile, in the 1930s the Soviet system
of <color=#3366CC>forced labour</color>, <color=#3366CC>expulsions</color> and <color=#3366CC>allegedly engineered famine</color> had a similar death toll. Millions of civilians were affected
by forced population transfers.
Recent history
The world wars ended the pre-eminent position of Britain, France and Germany in Europe and the world.
Cold War
The victors of World War II divided Europe into spheres of influence, with a Western Bloc and an <color=#3366CC>Eastern Bloc</color> of
countries opposing each other in the <color=#3366CC>Cold War</color>. The United States donated about $20 billion in <color=#3366CC>Marshall Plan</color> grants
and other funding to Western Europe, 1945 to 1951. The Soviet Union, concentrating on its own recovery, seized and
transferred most of Germany's industrial plants and exacted war reparations from, and imposed unfair trading
arrangements on, eastern European countries under its control.
The United States and the majority of European liberal democracies established the <color=#3366CC>NATO</color> military alliance in 1949.
With the aim of uniting and defending Western Europe, first steps toward economic and political <color=#3366CC>integration</color> began with
the <color=#3366CC>Council of Europe</color> (1949–), the <color=#3366CC>European Coal and Steel Community</color> (1952–2002) and <color=#3366CC>European Economic</color>
<color=#3366CC>Community</color> (1958–1993). The Soviet Union and its satellites established the <color=#3366CC>Warsaw Pact</color> in 1955.
The peak period of European decolonization occurred in the two decades following World War II. During this window,
European colonial powers began a <color=#3366CC>rapid withdrawal from their overseas territories</color>, starting with major Asian nations
like India (1947) and Indonesia (1949). In the "Year of Africa" (1960), 17 African nations gained independence in a
single year.
After decades of economic growth and an increase in the standard of living of its working class, Western Europe
experienced industrial decline, <color=#3366CC>oil-fueled inflation</color> and recession in the 1970s. Germany and Sweden sought to create a
social consensus behind a gradual restructuring while Britain implemented aggressive austerity and privatization.
Western Europe's remaining military dictatorships all collapsed in quick succession in the 1970s. In Portugal's 1974
<color=#3366CC>Carnation Revolution</color>, military officers overthrew the decades-old <color=#3366CC>Estado Novo</color> regime, beginning a transition to
democracy. Later that year, <color=#3366CC>Greece's military junta</color> collapsed over its role in the Cyprus crisis, restoring civilian rule in
the period known as the Metapolitefsi. The death of Spain's caudillo in 1975 set off a top-down <color=#3366CC>transition in Spain</color> led by
reformist politicians and <color=#3366CC>King Juan Carlos I</color> that replaced the old regime with a <color=#3366CC>constitutional monarchy</color>.
Post–Cold War era
Soviet leader <color=#3366CC>Mikhail Gorbachev</color> repudiated the Brezhnev Doctrine in the late 1980s and refused to intervene militarily
against <color=#3366CC>Solidarność</color>-led democratic reforms in Poland (1989), which led rapidly to <color=#3366CC>fall of the Berlin Wall</color>, the <color=#3366CC>collapse of</color>
<color=#3366CC>Communist governments outside the Soviet Union</color> and the end of the <color=#3366CC>Iron Curtain</color> that had divided Europe since the
end of World War II. In 1990 the <color=#3366CC>Federal Republic of Germany absorbed East Germany</color>. In 1991, the Soviet Union itself
<color=#3366CC>split into fifteen independent states</color>. The most <color=#3366CC>violent dissolution occurred in Yugoslavia</color>.
English computer scientist <color=#3366CC>Tim Berners-Lee</color>’s (1955–) invention of the <color=#3366CC>World Wide Web</color> while working at the <color=#3366CC>European</color>
<color=#3366CC>Organization for Nuclear Research</color> in Switzerland in 1989 began the transformation of the <color=#3366CC>Internet</color> from a specialized
research network for scholars into a global interconnected <color=#3366CC>information system</color> used by billions of people every day, and
the primary engine of the <color=#3366CC>Digital Revolution</color>.
In 1993, the <color=#3366CC>Maastricht Treaty</color> established the <color=#3366CC>European Union</color>, succeeding the <color=#3366CC>EEC</color>. The neutral countries of Austria,
Finland and Sweden joined the EU in 1995, and those that did not join were tied into the EU's economic market via the
European Economic Area and Schengen Agreement, which lifted border controls between member states. The <color=#3366CC>euro</color>
was created in 1999 and replaced all previous currencies in participating states in 2002, forming the eurozone. In 2004,
the EU gained 10 new members and two more in 2007. Public opinion in the EU turned against further enlargement. A
European Constitution was rejected by voters in 2005.
Russia <color=#3366CC>invaded Georgia</color> in 2008.
Touched off by the <color=#3366CC>Great Recession</color> and the <color=#3366CC>2008 financial crisis</color>, which caused government borrowing costs to soar,
the decade-long <color=#3366CC>euro area crisis</color> (2009–2018) was intensified by the structural inability of the most impacted countries
to devalue their <color=#3366CC>shared currency</color> and further aggravated by a continent-wide pivot toward austerity resulting in
widespread social unrest and the anti-austerity movement. In a referendum in the United Kingdom on the country's
membership in the EU in 2016, 52% of voters voted to leave the EU, leading to the complex <color=#3366CC>Brexit</color> separation process
and negotiations, which led to political and economic changes for both the UK and the remaining EU countries.
Although multiple European countries currently outside of the EU remain interested in joining, the aspiration of a
geographically and economically diminished EU to act as a third global superpower appeared increasingly unrealistic.
Beginning the <color=#3366CC>largest and deadliest war in Europe since World War II</color>, Russia invaded Ukraine on 24 February 2022,
vastly escalating an ongoing conflict that had started with the <color=#3366CC>2014 Russian annexation of Crimea</color> and <color=#3366CC>separatist</color>
<color=#3366CC>fighting in Donbas</color>. In response, <color=#3366CC>Finland</color> and <color=#3366CC>Sweden</color> became members of NATO in 2023 and in 2024.
Chronology
• 7000 BC: <color=#3366CC>Neolithic</color> in Europe begins.
• 4600 – 4200 BC: First European proto-civilisation, first golden artefacts and first fortified stone town – the Varna
culture.
• 5000 – 3500 BC: First European proto-script – the Old European script (Danubian script).
• 3850 – 3600 BC: Malta's Temple period begins.
• 3500 BC: First European civilization, <color=#3366CC>Minoan civilization</color>, begins on Crete.
• 3000 BC: <color=#3366CC>Indo-Europeans</color> begin a large-scale settlement of the continent.
• 2500 BC: <color=#3366CC>Stonehenge</color> is constructed.
• 2100 BC: First European script, Cretan hieroglyphs, is invented by Minoans.
• 1750 BC: <color=#3366CC>Mycenaean civilization</color> begins.
• 1600 BC: <color=#3366CC>Thera eruption</color> occurs on the island of <color=#3366CC>Santorini</color>, destructing the Minoan city of <color=#3366CC>Thera</color>.
• 1450 BC: <color=#3366CC>Crete</color> is conquered by <color=#3366CC>Mycenaeans</color>.
• 1200 BC: <color=#3366CC>Late Bronze Age collapse</color> begins, that may be seen in the context of a technological history that saw the
slow spread of ironworking technology from present-day Bulgaria and <color=#3366CC>Romania</color> in the 13th and the 12th centuries
BC.
• 1100 BC: <color=#3366CC>Minoan civilization</color> falls.
